concept.name: Parabolic decline
concept.definition: The inverted analogue of the parabolic advance: a downtrend that accelerates so successive sell-offs steepen and the price path curves downward like a downward-opening parabola, typically driven by panic, forced liquidation, or cascading stops. It is interpreted as a capitulation dynamic whose slope is unsustainable, with a tentative bullish-reversal signal when price breaks back above the curved trend line overhead. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Each wave of selling panics more holders into selling, so the fall keeps steepening — until everyone who could be forced out is out, and the collapse exhausts itself.
concept.mechanics: Identify a prevailing downtrend, connect the rally highs within it with a curving downward trend line, and watch for accelerating, gap-prone legs lower often on climactic volume. The reversal signal is a close back above the curved trend line, with a stop below the pattern's lower extreme; recoveries frequently retrace a large fraction of the decline, mirroring the upward arc's tendency to retrace.
concept.failure_modes: Falling knives: parabolic declines driven by genuine insolvency or fraud never recover, so 'unsustainable slope' is not a floor. Each re-steepening produces false rebound signals, and stops placed just above the curve are repeatedly run in volatile crashes.
concept.misconceptions: That a parabolic fall guarantees a V-shaped recovery — the exhaustion-bounce framing is a hypothesis, and many parabolic declines are the first leg of a longer bear market. It shares only a name with the Parabolic SAR indicator.
concept.example: A stock drops in three accelerating legs from $60 to $22, each bounce weaker, tracing a downward curve through the rally highs; when price finally closes back above the curve at $26 on heavy volume, the capitulation-reversal reading is triggered.
